12294: Ephesians: One New People in a World of Powers
12295:
Ephesians reads more like a prayer and a sermon than a crisis letter. It opens with one enormous sentence of praise (in Greek, Eph 1:3-14 is a single sentence) for God's plan 'to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth' (Eph 1:10). Its centre is a breathtaking claim: in the Messiah, God has torn down the wall between Jews and Gentiles and created 'one new humanity' (Eph 2:15), and this reconciled community is God's announcement to the spiritual powers that their divided order is ending (Eph 3:10). The second half turns this vision into ordinary life: speech, anger, sex, money, work, marriage, parenting, slavery and spiritual conflict.

The letter was written to people who lived in or near Ephesus, a great city of Roman Asia famous for the temple of Artemis, for magical practices, and for its devotion to the emperors. Many hearers had lived in fear of fate, stars and spirits. Ephesians tells them that the crucified and risen Messiah sits above 'every rule and authority and power' (Eph 1:21), and that they sit with him (Eph 2:6).

Western readers have often taken Ephesians as a handbook of individual salvation (chosen before time, saved by grace, armed for private battle). Those themes are there. But in its own setting the letter's focus is corporate: God's choice of a people in Christ, the creation of one body from enemies, a household reshaped by mutual submission, and a church standing together against the powers. This study traces those threads, presents the debates fairly, and names who holds which view.
12296: Read Ephesians as Israel's story widening to include the nations. Gentiles who were once 'alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise' (Eph 2:12) are now 'fellow citizens with the saints and members of the household of God' (Eph 2:19), built into a new temple where God lives by the Spirit. Election, inheritance, sealing, temple, peace to the far and the near, the divine council and its rebellious powers, the armour of God from Isaiah: all are Jewish categories. Grace (charis) is God's lavish gift that creates a people and calls for a 'worthy walk'; the church's unity is not a nice extra but the visible proof of the gospel.
12297: Chosen as a people in the Messiah
12298: Israel knew itself as chosen by love, not merit (Deut 7:6-8). Ephesians says God chose 'us in him': election happens in the Messiah, the chosen one, and is shared by all who are in him. Its aim is holiness and praise.
12299: The far and the near brought together
12300: Isaiah promised peace 'to the far and to the near'. Ephesians reads this as Gentiles (far) and Jews (near) reconciled to God and one another through the cross.
12302: The Jerusalem temple separated Jew from Gentile by a barrier. In the Messiah, Jews and Gentiles together become the holy temple where God dwells by his Spirit, built on the cornerstone of Isaiah 28.
12303: Grace that creates a new way of life
12304: Salvation is a gift 'not from works', yet it creates people 'for good works which God prepared beforehand'. Gift and grateful, faithful response belong together, as in covenant relationship.
12305: The powers and the divine council
12306: Jewish scripture and later Jewish writings pictured heavenly beings assigned to nations, some of whom rebelled. Ephesians announces that Christ is enthroned above them all, and that the church's unity makes God's wisdom known to them.
12308: Ancient households were the building blocks of society, ordered from the top down. Ephesians keeps the household but reshapes every relationship by mutual submission, self-giving love modelled on Christ, and the shared lordship of Christ over master and slave.
12310: The armour of Eph 6 is the armour Isaiah says God himself and his Messiah wear when coming to set things right. The church is clothed with God's character: truth, justice, peace, faithfulness.
12311: Gentile believers from civic and Artemis worship
12312: Whether they truly belong to Israel's God and his people; how to live in a city whose festivals, guilds and economy revolved around Artemis and the emperors.
12313: Converts from magic and fear of spirits
12314: Protection from hostile powers, fate and curses; whether Christ really rules over the forces they once tried to manipulate (Acts 19:18-19).
12316: How their heritage and covenants relate to the flood of Gentile believers; whether unity means losing Jewish identity.
12317: Wives, children and slaves in believing households
12318: Addressed directly as moral agents, unusual in ancient household teaching; how the gospel changes daily power relationships at home.
12319: Sister churches in Asia receiving a circulated copy
12320: If the letter was circular, churches such as Laodicea would hear it as a general charter for Gentile churches in the region (Col 4:16).
12322: Praise to the Father who chose, adopted, redeemed and sealed a people in the Messiah, with the plan of uniting all things in him.
12324: Paul prays they will grasp the power that raised Christ and seated him above every ruler and name, as head over all things for the church.
12325: From dead to raised with him
12326: Once dead in sins under the ruler of the power of the air; now made alive, raised and seated with Christ, by grace through faith, created for good works.
12328: Gentiles once far off are brought near. Christ is our peace: he broke down the dividing wall, created one new humanity, and built a temple for God.
12330: God's long-hidden secret is that Gentiles are fellow heirs, one body and sharers of the promise. Through the church God's wisdom is shown to the heavenly powers.
12332: Paul kneels before the Father of every family and prays they will know the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge.
12333: Walk worthy: one body, many gifts
12334: Keep the unity of the Spirit. One body, one Spirit, one Lord, one faith. The ascended Christ gives people-gifts to equip the church to grow up into him.
12335: Put off old, put on new
12336: Do not live like the Gentiles in futile thinking. Put on the new humanity created in God's likeness: truthful speech, honest work, kindness and forgiveness.
12338: Walk in love as Christ loved us; reject sexual immorality and greed; live as children of light; be filled with the Spirit in song and thanksgiving.
12340: Mutual submission out of reverence for Christ reshapes marriage, parenting and slavery, with Christ's self-giving love as the pattern and Christ as the one Lord of all.
12342: Be strong in the Lord. The real struggle is against the spiritual powers; stand firm clothed in God's own armour from Isaiah, praying in the Spirit.
12343: Every blessing in Christ, enthroned above the powers
12344: After a brief greeting 'to the saints who are [in Ephesus] and faithful in Christ Jesus', the letter bursts into praise. God has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ: he chose us in him before the foundation of the world to be holy, predestined us for adoption, redeemed and forgave us through his blood, made known the mystery of his will, his plan to unite all things in Christ, and gave us an inheritance. 'You also', the Gentile hearers, were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, the down payment of our inheritance. Paul then prays that they will know the hope of God's calling, the riches of his inheritance in the saints, and the surpassing power that raised Christ and seated him at God's right hand far above every ruler, authority, power and dominion, with all things under his feet, as head over all things for the church, his body.
12345: Who wrote Ephesians and to whom? The letter names Paul as author, in prison (Eph 3:1, Eph 4:1, Eph 6:20). Many critical scholars (Andrew Lincoln, Ernest Best, Margaret MacDonald) think a disciple of Paul wrote it a generation later, pointing to its long liturgical sentences, unusual vocabulary, its picture of a universal church, and its close parallels with Colossians. Others (Harold Hoehner, Frank Thielman, Clinton Arnold, Lynn Cohick) defend Paul's authorship, writing perhaps from Rome around AD 60-62. Also, the words 'in Ephesus' (Eph 1:1) are missing from several of the earliest manuscripts, including the papyrus P46 and the first hands of Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus. The letter also lacks personal greetings, strange if Paul had spent nearly three years in Ephesus (Acts 20:31). Many scholars therefore think it was a circular letter for several churches of Roman Asia; Marcion in the second century knew it as the letter 'to the Laodiceans', perhaps the letter mentioned in Col 4:16.
12346: Ephesus was the leading city of the Roman province of Asia, with perhaps 200,000 people, a great harbour and the famous temple of Artemis, one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Ephesian Artemis was honoured as a powerful protector, and the city was famous for magic: the 'Ephesian letters' (Ephesia grammata) were mystic words used as charms. People feared fate, the stars and spirits, and sought power to control them (Acts 19:18-19). Ephesians answers in kind: God's 'power', 'strength' and 'might' (Eph 1:19) are greater than all powers 'named' in this age and the next, perhaps a hint at the practice of invoking names in magic, as Clinton Arnold argues. Sealing was used for ownership and protection of goods; the 'down payment' (arrabōn) was a deposit guaranteeing full payment.
12347: The opening praise follows the pattern of a Jewish berakah, a blessing prayer that begins 'Blessed be God' and recounts his saving acts. Its themes are Israel's: chosen in love (Deut 7:6-8), adopted as sons, redeemed (the exodus word), given an inheritance (the land), sealed (compare the mark of Ezek 9:4) and made God's own possession (Exod 19:5). Now these gifts are given 'in the Messiah' to Jews ('we who first hoped in Christ', Eph 1:12) and to Gentiles ('you also', Eph 1:13). Christ's enthronement fulfils Ps 110:1 ('sit at my right hand') and Ps 8:6 (all things under the feet of humanity). The 'powers' recall the heavenly beings set over the nations in Deut 32:8-9 and the princes of Persia and Greece in Dan 10.
12348: Gentile believers who had once sought protection from Artemis or magical charms would hear that they are already blessed with 'every' blessing, chosen, adopted and sealed by the Spirit, and that the Christ they belong to rules over every power they once feared. They are not latecomers on probation; they share Israel's inheritance.
12349: The chapter starts with worship, not instructions: identity before behaviour. It reassures people who feel insecure in faith that their belonging rests on God's initiative in Christ. It also confronts modern fears (fate, chaos, hostile systems) with the claim that Christ already reigns over them.
12350: Israel chosen as God's treasured people out of love, not merit: the pattern for 'he chose us'.
12351: Israel as God's treasured possession; Ephesians speaks of God's own possession and inheritance.
12352: 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies your footstool': Christ's enthronement over the powers.
12353: 'You have put all things under his feet', applied to the Messiah as the true human.
12354: God divided the nations, with the Lord's own portion being his people; background for powers over the nations.
12355: Ephesians 1 teaches that God chose a fixed list of individuals before time, and the main question is whether I am on it.
12356: The language is plural and 'in him': God chose a people in the Messiah, now including Gentiles. Individual and corporate aspects are debated, but the passage was written to produce praise and assurance, not anxiety.
12357: Raised by grace; the dividing wall torn down
12358: You were dead in trespasses and sins, following the course of this world and the ruler of the power of the air; we all lived that way. But God, rich in mercy, made us alive together with Christ, raised us and seated us with him in the heavenly places. 'By grace you have been saved through faith... not from works, so that no one may boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.' Then: remember that you Gentiles were once without the Messiah, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, strangers to the covenants of promise, without hope and without God. Now you who were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ. He is our peace: he made the two one, broke down the dividing wall of hostility, abolished the law of commandments in ordinances, to create in himself one new humanity, reconciling both to God through the cross. You are no longer strangers but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God's household, built on the foundation of apostles and prophets, with Christ as cornerstone, a holy temple in the Lord.
12359: Herod's temple in Jerusalem had a stone balustrade (the soreg) around the inner courts. Signs in Greek and Latin warned Gentiles not to pass beyond it; Josephus describes them (Jewish War 5.193-194). A complete Greek example found in 1871 by Charles Clermont-Ganneau, now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums, says that any foreigner caught inside will have himself to blame for his death that follows. Paul himself was accused of bringing Trophimus the Ephesian past that barrier (Acts 21:27-29). Whether Eph 2:14 alludes directly to that barrier is debated (the Greek words differ), but the image of a wall dividing Jew from Gentile would have been vivid. If the letter is late, the temple had been destroyed in AD 70, which would add another layer.
12360: Citizenship in a Greek city (politeia) was a prized status; resident aliens (paroikoi) and strangers lived without full rights. Ephesians uses this civic language: Gentiles move from foreigners to fellow citizens and members of the household. 'Workmanship' (poiēma) means something made, a work of art or craft. The 'ruler of the power of the air' fits the ancient belief that the air between earth and heaven was inhabited by spirits.
12361: Jews commonly called Gentiles 'far' and Israel 'near' to God (Ps 148:14). Isaiah promised 'peace, peace to the far and to the near' (Isa 57:19) and the messenger 'who announces peace' (Isa 52:7); Ephesians weaves both into Christ who 'came and preached peace'. Gentiles are not added to a new Gentile religion; they are brought into Israel's commonwealth, covenants and hope. The temple image draws on Isa 28:16 (a tested cornerstone in Zion) and Ps 118:22. The 'law of commandments in ordinances' is abolished as a wall of hostility, its dividing function, which interpreters relate in different ways to the continuing goodness of the law (Eph 6:2 still quotes it).
12362: Gentiles who had lived 'without God in the world' (literally 'atheists', a word pagans also used of those who rejected their gods) would hear an astonishing reversal: from strangers to family, from outsiders to the very stones of God's temple. Jewish believers would hear that they are not losing their heritage but welcoming the nations into it, as the prophets foresaw.
12363: Ephesians 2 holds personal salvation (verses 1-10) and social reconciliation (verses 11-22) as one gospel. Churches divided along ethnic, racial or class lines contradict the cross, which 'killed the hostility'. For Gentile Christians it is also a reminder of humility and gratitude toward the Jewish people, into whose story they have been brought.
12364: Peace to the far and to the near: Gentiles and Jews reconciled.
12365: The feet of the one who brings good news and announces peace.
12366: A tested, precious cornerstone laid in Zion.
12367: The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.
12368: Ephesians 2:8-9 sums up the gospel: salvation is a private gift to individuals received by faith.
12369: It is a free gift by grace through faith, and verse 10 adds that it creates people for good works. Verses 11-22 show what that grace produces: one new humanity from former enemies. Salvation is personal and communal.
12370: The mystery made known and a prayer for love
12371: Paul, a prisoner of Christ for the sake of the Gentiles, explains the 'mystery' revealed to him and to the apostles and prophets: that the Gentiles are fellow heirs, members of the same body, and sharers in the promise in Christ through the gospel. Though the least of all the saints, he was given grace to preach the unsearchable riches of Christ to the Gentiles, so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly places. He urges them not to lose heart over his sufferings. Then he kneels before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, praying that they will be strengthened by the Spirit, that Christ may dwell in their hearts through faith, and that, rooted in love, they may grasp the breadth, length, height and depth of Christ's love that surpasses knowledge. He ends with a doxology to the one who can do far more than we ask or imagine.
12372: The chapter assumes Paul's imprisonment, traditionally the Roman house arrest of Acts 28:16-31, though Caesarea or an Ephesian imprisonment have been proposed. If written by a later disciple, it presents Paul as the model apostle to the Gentiles whose sufferings had borne fruit. The 'apostles and prophets' as recipients of revelation suggests an early generation of leaders now seen as a foundation (Eph 2:20).
12373: A 'family' (patria) in the ancient world was a lineage named after its father; Paul plays on Father (patēr) and every family (patria) named from him. The four dimensions (breadth, length, height, depth) may echo descriptions of cosmic or temple measurements, or magical formulas describing the extent of power, as Arnold suggests; their exact reference is debated. Kneeling to pray was a posture of intense supplication; Jews typically prayed standing.
12374: 'Mystery' recalls Daniel, where God reveals hidden things (raz) about his kingdom (Dan 2:28, Dan 2:47), and the Dead Sea Scrolls, where the 'mysteries of God' are his plans revealed to the community's teacher. The mystery here is not that Gentiles would be blessed (the prophets said they would, Isa 49:6), but the manner: as full co-heirs in one body without becoming Jews. The display of God's wisdom to the powers fits Jewish ideas of the heavenly court observing God's acts in history.
12375: Gentile believers could easily feel embarrassed that their apostle was in chains. Paul reframes his imprisonment as part of God's plan for their glory. The prayer would assure them that the love of Christ reaches every dimension of their lives.
12376: The church's very existence as a reconciled community is meant to be a sign, even to unseen powers, of God's wisdom. The prayer is a model: it asks not mainly for circumstances to change but for inner strength, deep love and knowledge of Christ.
12377: There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries: background to 'mystery' as revealed plan.
12378: The servant as a light to the nations, so that God's salvation reaches the ends of the earth.
12379: God's wisdom higher than heaven, deeper than Sheol, longer than the earth and broader than the sea.
12380: The mystery is something vague and spiritual that only the specially enlightened understand.
12381: In Paul's usage a mystery is God's plan once hidden and now openly announced; here it is specific: Gentiles as fellow heirs and one body with Jews in the Messiah.
12382: One body, many gifts, a new humanity
12383: Paul urges them to walk worthy of their calling with humility, gentleness, patience and love, eager to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace: one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all. Grace was given to each according to Christ's gift; quoting Ps 68 ('when he ascended on high he led captives and gave gifts to people'), he describes the ascended Christ giving apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers to equip the saints for ministry, so that the body grows to maturity and is not tossed by every wind of teaching. They must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in futility and darkness, but put off the old self and put on the new self created in God's likeness. Practical commands follow: speak truth, be angry without sinning, do not give the devil a foothold, stop stealing and work to share with the needy, speak only what builds up, do not grieve the Holy Spirit, put away bitterness and anger, be kind and forgive as God in Christ forgave you.
12384: Unity was under pressure in Gentile churches of Asia: differing teachings (Eph 4:14), cultural habits from pagan life, and the old tensions between Jews and Gentiles. The list of leaders (apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastor-teachers) reflects a church with recognised ministries; whether these are offices or functions, and whether apostles and prophets continue, is debated between traditions.
12385: Greek cities prized concord (homonoia) and orators often urged it, using the image of a body whose parts must cooperate; Paul uses the body image but makes Christ its head and source of growth. Pagan moralists also criticised Gentile vice. Theft by household slaves and labourers was a common complaint; Ephesians tells former thieves not only to stop but to work so they can give, turning a taker into a patron of the needy. 'Put off' and 'put on' evoke changing clothes, perhaps at baptism.
12386: The confession 'one God and Father of all' echoes the Shema (Deut 6:4), now expanded with one Lord, one Spirit. Ps 68:18 originally pictures God ascending Zion after victory, receiving gifts; Ephesians reads it as 'gave gifts'. Some Jewish traditions (such as the Aramaic Targum of the Psalms) also read 'gave' and linked the psalm to Moses ascending Sinai to receive Torah for Israel, associated with the feast of Shavuot (Pentecost); Ephesians may be drawing on such a reading, now applied to Christ giving the Spirit's gifts. Details of that background are debated. The ethical commands quote Zech 8:16 and Ps 4:4, and 'grieve the Holy Spirit' recalls Isa 63:10, where Israel grieved God's Spirit in the wilderness.
12387: New believers formed by pagan habits needed concrete guidance. Slaves and labourers would hear that their work could become a means of generosity. A church tempted by competing teachers would hear that maturity comes through the whole body using its gifts, not through spiritual elites.
12388: Unity is to be 'kept', not manufactured: it already exists in the one Spirit, and must be guarded by humility and patience. Ministry belongs to all the saints, with leaders equipping them. The new self is visible in ordinary speech, anger management, honest work and forgiveness.
12389: God ascends on high leading captives; Ephesians reads it of Christ giving gifts.
12390: The Shema, behind 'one Lord... one God and Father of all'.
12391: Speak the truth to one another.
12392: Be angry, and do not sin.
12393: Israel rebelled and grieved God's Holy Spirit.
12394: Ministry is what pastors and professional leaders do; ordinary believers receive it.
12395: Leaders are given 'to equip the saints for the work of ministry'. Every member has grace given to them, and the body builds itself up in love as each part works properly.
12396: Walk in love and light; submitting to one another
12397: Be imitators of God as beloved children, and walk in love as Christ loved us and gave himself as a fragrant offering. Sexual immorality, impurity, greed and coarse talk must not even be named among them; the greedy person is an idolater. Once darkness, they are now light in the Lord: walk as children of light, expose the unfruitful works of darkness, make the most of the time. Do not get drunk with wine, but be filled with the Spirit, speaking in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs, giving thanks, and submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ. Wives, to your husbands as to the Lord, for the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is head of the church. Husbands, love your wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, to make her holy; love them as your own bodies. Quoting Gen 2:24, Paul says this is a great mystery, and he is speaking about Christ and the church.
